articles.h1: Vetster review: what Vetster's own pages say about price, appointments and prescriptions
articles.lede: Quick answer: Vetster is a marketplace where you book a licensed veterinarian for a video appointment, 24/7. On its own published numbers there are two ways to pay - Vetster Plus at $12/month billed annually, which includes 4 same-day video appointments a year, or a single appointment starting at $102 one-time. Both options include 48-hour follow-up live messaging with your vet and prescriptions through VetsterRx. Prescribing is always the veterinarian's decision and depends on your state's rules, and Vetster states online vets are not a replacement for emergency clinics. Every figure below was read from vetster.com on 2026-09-26.

faqs.q: How much does Vetster cost?
faqs.a: Vetster Plus is $12/month, billed annually. Twelve months at that published price comes to $144 (12 x $12, arithmetic on Vetster's own figure) and it includes 4 same-day video appointments a year plus unlimited messaging with registered vet techs. A single appointment starts at $102 one-time at marketplace rates. Products, pharmacy fees and shipping are charged separately.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Vetster Plus and paying per appointment?
faqs.a: Vetster Plus is a yearly subscription: 4 same-day video appointments a year, 50% off additional bookings, up to 2 unused appointments carried over, unlimited messaging with registered vet techs, all pets under one plan. Paying per appointment buys one visit for one pet at marketplace rates, starting at $102 one-time, with the 48-hour follow-up messaging included.

faqs.q: Can a Vetster vet prescribe medication?
faqs.a: Yes, when a valid vet-client-patient relationship is in place and the condition can be handled safely over video. Whether that relationship can be established online depends on your state's rules, federal guidance often expects a real exam first, and prescribing is always the veterinarian's decision. The prescription is then sent to the pharmacy you choose - Vetster is not a pharmacy.

faqs.q: What are Vetster's pharmacy and shipping fees?
faqs.a: Pharmacy fee per order: $7 for Vetster Plus members, $14 for non-members. Compounding fee per medication: $10 for members, $20 for non-members. Standard shipping (2-3 business days) is free for members and for non-member orders over $45; express shipping (1-2 business days) is $19 for everyone.

faqs.q: Is Vetster available in my state?
faqs.a: Both payment options are listed as available in all states, and VetsterRx fulfillment is listed as available in all 50 States. Whether a vet can prescribe during an online visit still depends on your state's rules, so that is confirmed during the appointment itself.

faqs.q: When should I not use an online vet?
faqs.a: Go in person immediately for difficulty breathing, uncontrolled bleeding, collapse or seizures, severe or sudden pain, suspected poisoning, major trauma, or being unable to urinate. Vetster states online vets are not a replacement for emergency clinics and that an online vet will direct you to appropriate in-person care.

faqs.q: How long can I message my vet after the appointment?
faqs.a: 48-hour follow-up live messaging with your vet is included in both payment options. Vetster Plus separately includes unlimited messaging with registered vet techs for help with pet health, behaviour, nutrition and urgent advice.

faqs.q: What does this Vetster review check, and what does it not check?
faqs.a: It checks only what Vetster publishes on its own pages - the subscription price, the single-appointment price, the VetsterRx fee table, the prescribing rules and the emergency list - each with its source link and check date of 2026-09-26. It does not test-drive appointments, and it does not repeat prices from third-party comparison sites.

articles.disclaimer: Editorial review of Vetster's own published pages - not veterinary advice and not a paid endorsement. Prices, inclusions and fees change, so every figure carries its official source link and a check date of 2026-09-26; re-read the official page before you pay. Nothing here is a diagnosis: in an emergency, go to a clinic.

blocks.h2: How this review is built
blocks.html:
There is no independent score for an online vet service, and we will not invent one. This Vetster review reads only Vetster's own pages: the Vetster Plus page (price, inclusions, billing and cancellation FAQ), the VetsterRx pharmacy page (the full fee table) and Vetster's two wellness guides (how virtual care works, and how prescriptions work). Every number in the table below carries a link to the page it was read from and a check date.

Where Vetster does not publish something - for example, what a single appointment costs beyond the printed starting price, or how long a subscription has been running for a given pet - this page says not published on the official page instead of guessing.

blocks.h2: Vetster Plus vs a single appointment - published figures only
What the numbers say side by side
blocks.html:
The subscription and the single visit are priced on different units, so compare the units first. Vetster prints $12/month and then states in its own FAQ that billing occurs annually, once per year. A single appointment is printed as a one-time starting price of $102 and billed at whatever the chosen veterinarian's marketplace rate is - that is why the table says starting at and not costs.

The fee table is where the two options quietly diverge. The same pharmacy page prints both rates side by side: $7 vs $14 per order, $10 vs $20 per compounding, free standard shipping vs free only above $45. Express shipping is $19 either way.

blocks.h2: Where an online vet stops
blocks.html:
Vetster is explicit about the boundary, and a review that hides it would be useless. Its own guide says to seek immediate in-person or emergency care for seven signs: difficulty breathing, uncontrolled bleeding, collapse or seizures, severe or sudden pain, suspected poisoning, major trauma, and being unable to urinate. Its preparation guide repeats the point in different words - telehealth is not a substitute for emergency care.

Prescribing sits in the middle. Vetster's prescription guide says a valid vet-client-patient relationship is required in almost every state, that the open question is whether that relationship can be built over video, that federal guidance often expects a real exam first, and that prescribing is always the veterinarian's decision. Practical consequence for a reviewer: the appointment can end with "your pet needs to be seen in person", and that is the clinic standard, not a runaround.

articles.h1: Online vet vs in-person vet: when a video visit is enough and when you must go to a clinic
articles.lede: Quick answer: book an online vet for quick answers, after-hours questions, follow-up care, chronic-condition management, preventive care and medication questions. Go in person immediately - before any video call - if your pet has difficulty breathing, uncontrolled bleeding, collapses or seizes, has severe or sudden pain, suspected poisoning, major trauma, or is unable to urinate. A prescription is a separate question: it needs a valid vet-client-patient relationship, and whether that can be built over video depends on your state's rules.

faqs.q: Are online vets real veterinarians?
faqs.a: Yes. Vetster states that online vets are licensed veterinarians who have completed accredited veterinary training, and that they complete the same education and licensing process as all veterinarians.

faqs.q: When should I use an online vet instead of going in person?
faqs.a: For quick answers when something has changed with your pet, after hours when physical clinics are closed, follow-up care, chronic condition management, preventive recommendations, medication questions and quality-of-life discussions - plus the everyday clusters Vetster lists: skin, ear and eye concerns, digestive and urinary changes, behaviour, mobility and ongoing care.

faqs.q: When should I go straight to a clinic or emergency hospital?
faqs.a: Immediately, if your pet has difficulty breathing, uncontrolled bleeding, collapses or seizes, shows severe or sudden pain, is suspected of poisoning, has suffered major trauma, or is unable to urinate. Vetster also states plainly that telehealth is not a substitute for emergency care.

faqs.q: Can an online vet prescribe medication?
faqs.a: Only when a valid vet-client-patient relationship is in place and the condition is appropriate for virtual care. Whether that relationship can be built over video depends on state rules, federal guidance often expects a real exam first, and prescribing is always the veterinarian's decision. The prescription then goes to the pharmacy you choose.

faqs.q: What can an online vet not do?
faqs.a: They cannot perform a hands-on exam, and Vetster's own guidance puts conditions needing lab work or imaging, complex or serious illnesses, medications requiring close monitoring, higher-risk drugs and many controlled substances on the in-person side of the line.

faqs.q: Do I need my pet on camera during the appointment?
faqs.a: Yes, for as much of the appointment as possible. Vetster explains that the vet relies on what they can see on screen, that having your pet present creates the basis for the veterinary-client-patient relationship, and that without your pet on screen the vet may be unable to diagnose or prescribe.

faqs.q: Is there such a thing as a free online vet?
faqs.a: General pet information is widely available for free, but Vetster states that personalized care from a licensed veterinarian is typically a paid service, because licensed veterinarians are legally responsible for the care they provide.

blocks.h2: How this page is built
blocks.html:
The online vet vs in-person question is usually answered with opinions. This page answers it with one brand's published rules: Vetster runs both a telemedicine marketplace and a preparation guide written by its editorial team and verified by its own veterinarians, and it publishes exactly when it sends people to a clinic instead. Both columns below come from those pages - nothing is filled in from forums or comparison sites.

One honest limitation: the right-hand column is thinner than the left, because Vetster publishes its own side of the story and does not publish clinic prices or clinic opening hours. Those cells say not published on the official Vetster pages checked for this row rather than borrowing a number from somewhere else.

blocks.h2: Online vet vs in-person - the conditions side by side
The decision in one picture
blocks.html:
Run the urgent list first, everything else second. Vetster's seven emergency signs come before any other consideration, and its preparation guide repeats the principle: many people use virtual care precisely to find out whether their pet needs in-person or emergency care.

Then split by what the vet can actually do through a screen. Symptoms, history, photos, movement on camera, medication questions and follow-ups travel well over video. Lab work, imaging, a hands-on exam and higher-risk prescribing do not - and Vetster's own two-column table draws that line for you.

blocks.h2: The prescription question, which is where the confusion lives
blocks.html:
Three separate layers decide whether you leave an online visit with medication. First the relationship: almost every state requires a valid vet-client-patient relationship before any vet can prescribe, and Vetster says the open question is whether that relationship can be established over video. Second the federal picture: for many prescription medications, federal guidance expects the relationship to rest on a real exam or visit. Third the judgment: Vetster's guide says prescribing is always the veterinarian's decision, and a vet may still ask for a hands-on exam, lab work or imaging first.

If the prescription does happen, the pharmacy is your choice - Vetster states it is not a pharmacy and sends the script directly to the local or online pharmacy you pick, with the service fee shown as a labelled line item before checkout.

articles.h1: How to buy pet prescription meds online legally: the vet authorization step comes first
articles.lede: Quick answer: you cannot buy a prescription pet medication online legally without your veterinarian's authorization, and both pharmacies say so in their own words. Chewy Pharmacy states it can only dispense medication with a valid, patient-specific prescription from a licensed veterinarian; 1-800-PetMeds states that all prescription medications must have an authorization before they are dispensed. The buying itself is three steps: add the medication to the cart, enter your pet's and your vet clinic's details at checkout, and choose how the pharmacy gets the script - they contact your vet, or you mail a written one in. Then the clock: Chewy prints prescription processing within 24-48 hours after the pharmacy receives a valid script and delivery in 3-5 days once it is approved; 1-800-PetMeds prints vet approval required before shipment and standard delivery in 2-5 business days. Every number below was read from chewy.com and 1800petmeds.com on 2026-09-26.

faqs.q: Is it legal to buy pet medication online?
faqs.a: Yes, when the pharmacy dispenses against a valid prescription from a licensed veterinarian - that is the legal line both pharmacies describe. Chewy Pharmacy states it can only dispense medication with a valid, patient-specific prescription from a licensed veterinarian, and its compounding pharmacy states it is licensed in Kentucky and in every state it ships compounded medication to. 1-800-PetMeds states all prescription medications must have an authorization before they are dispensed.

faqs.q: Do I need the prescription in hand before I order?
faqs.a: At Chewy, no. Its FAQ says a written prescription is not required when you place the order; you pick at checkout whether Chewy contacts your vet or you mail the script, and the prescription has to be on file before dispensing. 1-800-PetMeds does not publish that ordering detail on the pages checked - it publishes that vet approval is required before shipment, so we leave that cell empty rather than guessing.

faqs.q: How long does the whole order take?
faqs.a: Chewy prints two windows: prescriptions are typically processed within 24-48 hours after the pharmacy receives a valid prescription, and delivery takes 3-5 days once the prescription is approved (a mailed paper prescription typically ships within 1-2 days after receipt). 1-800-PetMeds prints standard delivery in 2-5 business days with vet approval required before shipment.

faqs.q: What if my vet gives me a paper prescription?
faqs.a: At Chewy, place the order and choose mail-in prescription at checkout, then send the original - not a copy - with your order number to Chewy Pharmacy, 3621 Fern Valley Rd., Louisville, KY 40219 (Gabapentin orders: 360 Research Drive, Pittston, PA 18640); Chewy covers overnight shipping for it. At 1-800-PetMeds, mail it to Attn: Pharmacy, 420 S Congress Ave. #100, Delray Beach, FL 33445 with your phone or order number, or have your vet call 1-888-738-6331.

faqs.q: Are these the same drugs my vet sells?
faqs.a: Chewy says it sells the same FDA-approved meds as veterinary clinics and that its licensed pharmacy team checks each medication in the order. 1-800-PetMeds says it sells only U.S. FDA/EPA-approved medications - the same exact medications sold by your veterinarian - and that its products and facilities are regularly inspected by state agencies.

faqs.q: Can I set up refills for a chronic condition?
faqs.a: Chewy says that with valid refills on file at Chewy Pharmacy you can set up Autoship for the medication. 1-800-PetMeds' help page describes adding a prescription item to AutoShip: the pharmacy reaches out to your veterinarian for approval before shipping, and that request does not delay the existing AutoShip order.

faqs.q: What does compounded medication mean?
faqs.a: Chewy defines compounding as licensed pharmacists mixing or changing one or more FDA-approved medications to make a customized medication for a pet - for example a liquid instead of a tablet, or a strength that is not commercially available. Chewy states that all compounding ingredients are sourced from FDA registered manufacturers and distributors.

faqs.q: What does this page not cover?
faqs.a: It covers only what Chewy and 1-800-PetMeds publish on their own pages - authorization rules, mail-in addresses, processing and delivery windows, fees the pages actually print, and contact hours - each with its source link and a check date of 2026-09-26. It does not quote prices from marketplaces, does not compare every online pet pharmacy, and is not veterinary advice.

Shipping windows and policies change, so every figure carries its official source link and a check date of 2026-09-26; re-read the official page before you order. Medication decisions belong with your veterinarian.

blocks.h2: How this guide is built
blocks.html:
There is no independent licence-check database for online pet pharmacies that we can quote honestly, so this page does not invent one. It reads two pharmacies' own words: Chewy's pharmacy page and the FAQ printed on a Chewy prescription item, plus the 1-800-PetMeds help page. Every row below links to the page it came from and carries a check date.

Where a pharmacy does not publish something, the cell says not published on the official site. Two of those exist on purpose: Chewy does not print a shipping price on the pharmacy page we read, and 1-800-PetMeds does not print how long a received prescription takes to process.

blocks.h2: The three steps, then the clock
blocks.html:
The order itself is short; the authorization is the part that makes it legal. Chewy publishes the sequence as three steps: add your pet's meds with a click, enter a few quick details at checkout (your pet's information and your vet clinic's details so the pharmacy can verify the prescription with your vet), and let the pharmacy do the rest - its licensed pharmacy team reviews the prescription medications in the order to make sure they are safe and accurate for your pet.

Then two clocks run. Chewy prints a 24-48 hour processing window after the pharmacy receives a valid prescription and a 3-5 day delivery window after approval. 1-800-PetMeds prints the approval gate first - vet approval is required before shipment - and then standard delivery in 2-5 business days, with free shipping on orders over $49.

blocks.h2: Chewy vs 1-800-PetMeds: what each pharmacy publishes
The four things people get wrong
blocks.html:
Approval is not shipping. 1-800-PetMeds puts vet approval before shipment in the same sentence as its delivery window, so a fast shipping estimate means nothing until your vet signs off. Chewy separates them too: processing time starts when the valid prescription reaches the pharmacy, delivery time starts when it is approved.

Mail-in means the original. Chewy states plainly that it requires the original paper prescription, not a copy, and that your order number must be on it to avoid delays - and Gabapentin orders go to a different address in Pittston, PA. 1-800-PetMeds asks for your phone number or order number on anything mailed to its Delray Beach pharmacy.

Compounded is not the same as manufactured. Chewy defines compounding as licensed pharmacists mixing or changing one or more FDA-approved medications, and it states its compounding pharmacy is licensed in Kentucky and in each state it ships to, with PCAB accreditation.

Authorization is recorded. 1-800-PetMeds stores written and faxed prescriptions electronically and records phone authorizations, which is why the vet can call the pharmacy line directly instead of sending you paperwork.

faqs.q: What is the best joint supplement for dogs?
faqs.a: There is no independent ranking to quote, so this page picks from what the brands publish: Cosequin Soft Chews with MSM and Omega-3 for everyday use, Cosequin Chewable Tablets with MSM for dogs that prefer a tablet, Cosequin for Small Dogs for 5-25 lb dogs, Dasuquin Soft Chews for the ASU formula, Dasuquin Soft Chews for Senior Dogs and Dasuquin Advanced when your vet wants the veterinarian-exclusive formula. Cosequin's own guide says the decision starts with a visit to your veterinarian.

faqs.q: How much glucosamine does my dog need?
faqs.a: Both brands dose by body weight rather than a single number. Cosequin's table gives 1 soft chew a day (600 mg glucosamine) for a 10-29 lb dog for the first 4-6 weeks, then 1 every other day; 2 a day then 1 for 30-59 lb; 3 a day then 1-2 for 60 lb and over. Dasuquin instead sells a small-to-medium formula at 600 mg per chew and a large formula at 900 mg per chew. Your veterinarian sets the final amount.

faqs.q: Do I have to ask my vet first?
faqs.a: Both brands say so in their own words. Cosequin's guide says to schedule a visit with your veterinarian before deciding which joint supplement to give your dog, because the vet will evaluate your dog and provide a recommendation for your pet's needs. Dasuquin's directions say to consult your veterinarian to determine which formula is right for your dog.

faqs.q: Which ingredients should I look for?
faqs.a: Cosequin's guide tells buyers to research what is in the product and names high-quality ingredients like glucosamine and chondroitin sulfate as the ones that help support joint health. Both products carry those two; Cosequin adds MSM, omega-3s and (in the chewable) manganese, while Dasuquin adds avocado/soybean unsaponifiables, Boswellia serrata extract and green tea extract.

faqs.q: How long does the label say to give it?
faqs.a: Both brands publish an initial loading period of 4-6 weeks followed by a maintenance level - for example Cosequin's soft chew drops from 2 a day to 1 a day for a 30-59 lb dog after the initial phase, and Dasuquin's senior table does the same. That is the brands' own instruction window; it is not a promise of results and not a substitute for your veterinarian's advice.

faqs.q: How much do these cost?
faqs.a: Cosequin's official site publishes no prices: the homepage lists products and a Where to Buy call to action instead of price figures, and each product page ends in a SHOP HERE button. Dasuquin's catalog does the same with a WHERE TO BUY link. This page therefore shows no prices rather than filling the gap with marketplace numbers.

faqs.q: Which one for a small dog or a senior dog?
faqs.a: For a small dog, Cosequin's omega-3 soft chew page says dogs under 10 lbs should use Cosequin for Small Dogs - a 45 count with 260 mg glucosamine per chew, dosed 1 a day for a 5-10 lb dog initially and 1 every other day after the first 4-6 weeks. For senior dogs both brands publish a dedicated formula: Cosequin for Senior Dogs adds beta-glucans, and Dasuquin for Senior Dogs adds alpha-lipoic acid plus 80 mg of omega-3s per chew.

faqs.q: What does this list check, and what does it not check?
faqs.a: It checks only what Cosequin and Dasuquin publish on their own pages - per-serving ingredient milligrams, weight-based dosing tables, quality-check counts, manufacturing claims, availability and the absence of prices - each with a source link and a check date of 2026-09-26. It does not run lab tests, does not rank the whole market (many brands publish no usable label data on their own sites) and does not quote marketplace prices.

blocks.h2: Cosequin vs Dasuquin - published label figures only
